newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO to boycott most multilateral negotiations.
newsitem.headline: PLO to boycott most multilateral negotiations.

text.p: The PLO will boycott most multilateral peace talks to protest Israel's delay in implementing PLO-Israel interim peace deals signed last year, PLO officials said on Tuesday.
Near the West Bank town of Hebron, the focus of Arab-Israeli wrangling, two Israeli soldiers were wounded on Tuesday when a petrol bomb was thrown at their vehicle, security sources said.

"The Palestinian Authority decided...that its delegations will boycott all multilateral talks, except those tackling the refugees issue, as a protest against lack of progress in bilateral peace talks as a result of Israel's lack of seriousness in implementing interim accords," Jamil al-Tarifi, Palestinian Minister of Civil Affairs, told Reuters.

Palestinians fear Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ousted Israel's previous centre-left government in May elections, is bent on scrapping the peace process based on trading occupied Arab land for peace.
Netanyahu, who opposes trading land for peace, says he will nonetheless implement agreements signed between the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) and Israel's former government.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu paid his first official visit to a Jewish settlement in the West Bank in a show of defiance to Palestinians opposed to his policy of expanding such outposts.
Netanyahu, who opposes creation of a Palestinian state, has approved building thousands of new homes in the settlements.

"What, you don't understand that there were elections in Israel? The Arab world doesn't understand that there were elections in Israel?...And why not develop communities here?" Netanyahu said to reporters.

PLO officials said the boycott would last until progress is achieved in talks on implementing signed agreements on issues such as Israel's handover of most of Hebron and further West Bank redeployments and dates were set for resumption of final status peace talks.

Multilateral talks on five topics -- economic cooperation, water, the environment, arms control and refugees -- have been held since the Middle East peace talks were launched between Israel and the Palestinians, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan in 1991.
Syria and Lebanon from the outset boycotted the multilateral forums saying Israel should not be integrated into the region until there was progress in the bilateral negotiations.

PLO negotiator Hassan Asfour said co-sponsors of the peace process, the United States and Russia, as well as Europe and Arab states -- all of which participate in the multilaterals -- had been notified of the Palestinian Authority's decision.

For the past two months, PLO and Israeli negotiators have struggled to close a deal on implementing Israel's handover of most of Hebron to the Palestinian Authority. The petrol bomb thrown in the area on Tuesday was the latest incident in what has long been a flashpoint of Arab-Israeli violence.
The sides accuse each other of delaying an agreement.
"If he (Netanyahu) thinks that I will accept his conditions or I will make concessions, he is wrong," Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told reporters in the West Bank city of Bethlehem.
Netanyahu told reporters at Ariel settlement in the West Bank: "We're not impressed by the threats but we are impressed with the fact that they don't want to conclude an agreement."
Israel wants to alter the Hebron accord to guarantee additional security for the 400 Jews living and studying in the city amidst more than 100,000 Palestinians.

Under a interim PLO-Israel deal, Israel was to hand over seven major West Bank towns to the PLO. It handed over six. The Hebron pullout was delayed by a wave of Moslem militant suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March.
